steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on BP-DeepONet, a physics-informed DeepONet method for cuffless estimation of arterial blood pressure waveforms. Motivate the medical problem, review deep learning approaches and their limitation, explain our approach, and list our contributions.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) says cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death globally. In 2019, about 32% of all global deaths were caused by CVDs, and most of these deaths were due to heart attack and stroke. There is enough evidence to say that high blood pressure (or hypertension) is the predominant cause of CVDs. In practice, the morphology of the arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveforms can reflect the cardiovascular status of humans. So it is very important to monitor ABP waveforms continuously in order to detect and prevent diseases.

In the clinical setting the gold standard for monitoring ABP waveforms is the invasive method, where an invasive pressure sensor is implanted into the artery. The invasive method is very risky and the devices used are expensive. It is commonly used in intensive care units (ICUs). The non-invasive method on the other hand is a more desirable choice for monitoring ABP waveforms daily.

In recent years deep learning-based methods for non-invasive ABP waveform estimation have attracted huge research interest. These methods usually estimate the ABP from other physiological signals that are much easier to measure. The most commonly used signals are the electrocardiogram (ECG) and the photoplethysmogram (PPG). The ECG signal records the heart’s electrical activity through cardiac cycles. It is measured by electrodes which can detect the small electrical changes that come from the cardiac activity. Patterns in ECG signals can indicate many cardiac abnormalities. The PPG signal is an optical signal that can detect blood volume changes in the microvascular bed of tissue. It is often obtained by illuminating the skin with a pulse oximeter and measuring the changes in light absorption. Figure 1 shows examples of filtered ECG and PPG signals.

Deep learning models were first introduced to estimate systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Later more complicated neural networks were used to estimate the whole ABP waveform. One study proposed a neural network made of a convolutional neural network (CNN), a bi-directional gated recurrent unit (Bi-GRU), and attention layers to estimate ABP from ECG and PPG. Another proposed a network that predicts ABP using only PPG signals. A third work introduced a modified transformer-based model that predicts the ABP waveform from ECG, PPG, and some extracted morphological features.

All of the models above are trained in a data-driven way, which means they are trained by minimizing the difference between the ground truth label and the network prediction. The labeled data is usually measured with invasive methods in the radial artery, so the trained neural network will only predict the radial ABP waveform. But ABP waveforms are different at different locations in the arterial system (See Figure 2), and radial waveforms may not be enough to diagnose CVD and reflect the status of the cardiovascular system. For example, some studies showed that the brachial waveform is more valuable than the radial waveform for assessing cardiac contractility. Another important observation is the pulse pressure amplification effect. Pulse pressure is the difference between the maximum and minimum of the pressure waveforms, and this difference increases as the pulse wave propagates through the arterial system. All the current deep learning-based algorithms can only predict radial ABP waveforms, because they are trained with labeled data measured at the radial artery.

In this work we want to develop new methods that predict ABP waveforms at different locations and at all times in the artery, conditioned on the physical law that governs blood flow, which is the Navier-Stokes equation. We use the physics-informed DeepONet (PI-DeepONet). DeepONet was first proposed to learn the solution operator that maps variable inputs to the corresponding latent solutions of some partial differential equation (PDE) systems, and its training is entirely data-driven. If the underlying PDE system is given explicitly, the PDE can be put into the training loss, like in physics-informed neural networks (PINN). A DeepONet trained like this is called a physics-informed DeepONet. In the arterial system the hemodynamics, i.e. the blood flow dynamics, can be modeled and simulated with the Navier-Stokes equation. So we can put the Navier-Stokes equation into the training loss and learn the solution operator that maps physiological signals to solutions of the corresponding PDEs. In our setting the spatial domain of the Navier-Stokes equation is a segment of the artery, and the labeled data can be used as a Dirichlet boundary condition. After giving the other necessary initial/boundary conditions we can identify the PDE solution in the whole domain. This way we get the ABP waveforms at different locations and at all times.

Our main contributions are:

- 1. This work is the first attempt to apply physics-informed operator learning to ABP waveform estimation. Our methods are the first to predict ABP waveforms at different locations in the artery conditioned by the physical law that governs blood flow, the Navier-Stokes equation. The methods force the neural network solutions to satisfy a 1-D Navier-Stokes equation with a Windkessel boundary condition and a time-periodic condition. The Windkessel boundary condition can simulate physical reflection waves.

- 2. Our methods can predict blood pressure waveforms with reasonably good accuracy and keep some physical properties like pulse pressure amplification.

- 3. As far as we know, our methods are the first that incorporate variable time-periodic conditions into DeepONet. We also propose an effective implementation method for training the network.

- 4. We also incorporate meta-learning into training so that model hyper-parameters are estimated automatically from the input physiological signals.

- 5. During training we only need the blood pressure measurement at the outlet side of the domain, and no extra measurement is needed.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death globally [1]. In 2019, about 32% of all global deaths were caused by CVDs, the majority of them due to heart attack and stroke. There is sufficient evidence to support that high blood pressure (or hypertension) is the predominant cause of CVDs [2]. In practice, the morphology of arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveforms can reflect the cardiovascular status of humans [3,4,5,6]. Therefore, it is of great importance to monitor ABP waveforms continuously to detect and prevent diseases.

In the clinical setting, the gold standard for ABP waveform monitoring is the invasive method, which involves implanting an invasive pressure sensor into the artery. The invasive method is very risky, and the devices used are expensive; it is commonly used in intensive care units (ICUs). The non-invasive method, on the other hand, is a more desirable choice for the daily monitoring of ABP waveforms.

Deep learning-based methods for non-invasive ABP waveform estimation have attracted huge research interest in recent years. These methods usually estimate the ABP from other physiological signals that are much easier to measure, most commonly the electrocardiogram (ECG) and the photoplethysmogram (PPG). The ECG signal records the heart’s electrical activity through cardiac cycles. It is measured by electrodes that detect the small electrical changes resulting from cardiac activity, and its patterns can indicate many cardiac abnormalities. The PPG signal is an optical signal that can detect blood volume changes in the microvascular bed of tissue. It is often obtained by illuminating the skin with a pulse oximeter and measuring changes in light absorption. Examples of filtered ECG and PPG signals are shown in Figure 1.

Deep learning models were introduced to estimate systolic and diastolic blood pressure in [7]. Then, more complicated neural networks were used to estimate the entire ABP waveform [8,9,10]. In [8], the authors proposed a neural network consisting of a convolutional neural network (CNN), a bi-directional gated recurrent unit (Bi-GRU), and attention layers to estimate ABP from ECG and PPG. In [9], a network predicting ABP only from PPG signals was proposed. In [10], the authors introduced a modified transformer-based model to predict the ABP waveform from ECG, PPG, and some extracted morphological features.

The models above are all trained in a data-driven way, i.e., by minimizing the difference between the ground truth label and the network prediction. Since the labeled data is usually measured by invasive methods in the radial artery [11], the trained neural network will only predict the radial ABP waveform. However, ABP waveforms differ at different locations in the arterial system [12,13] (See Figure 2), and radial waveforms may not be sufficient to diagnose CVD and reflect the status of the cardiovascular system. For example, some studies have shown that the brachial waveform is more valuable than the radial waveform when assessing cardiac contractility [14,15]. Another important observation is the pulse pressure amplification effect: pulse pressure is defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum of the pressure waveforms, and this difference increases as the pulse wave propagates through the arterial system. All current deep learning-based algorithms can only predict radial ABP waveforms, since they are trained with labeled data measured at the radial artery.

In this work, we aim to develop new methods to predict ABP waveforms at different locations and at all times in the artery, conditioned on the physical law that governs blood flow, i.e., the Navier-Stokes equation. We use the physics-informed DeepONet (PI-DeepONet) [16]. DeepONet was initially proposed to learn the solution operator mapping variable inputs to the corresponding latent solutions of certain partial differential equation (PDE) systems [17], and its training process is entirely data-driven. If the underlying PDE system is explicitly given, the PDE can be incorporated into the training loss as in physics-informed neural networks (PINN) [18]; a DeepONet trained this way is called a physics-informed DeepONet. In the arterial system, the hemodynamics, i.e., blood flow dynamics, can be modeled and simulated by the Navier-Stokes equation [19,20,21]. We can therefore incorporate the Navier-Stokes equation into the training loss and learn the solution operator that maps physiological signals to solutions of the corresponding PDEs. In our setting, the spatial domain of the Navier-Stokes equation is a segment of the artery, and the labeled data serves as a Dirichlet boundary condition. Given the other necessary initial/boundary conditions, we can identify the PDE solution in the whole domain, and consequently obtain the ABP waveforms at different locations and at all times.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

- 1. This work is the first attempt to apply physics-informed operator learning to ABP waveform estimation. The proposed methods are the first to predict ABP waveforms at different locations in the artery conditioned by the physical law that governs blood flow, i.e., the Navier-Stokes equation. They enforce neural network solutions to satisfy a 1-D Navier-Stokes equation with a Windkessel boundary condition and a time-periodic condition, where the Windkessel boundary condition can simulate physical reflection waves.

- 2. The proposed methods predict blood pressure waveforms with reasonably good accuracy and preserve physical properties such as pulse pressure amplification.

- 3. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed methods are the first to incorporate variable time-periodic conditions into DeepONet. We also propose an effective implementation method for network training.

- 4. We incorporate meta-learning into the training to estimate model hyper-parameters automatically from the input physiological signals.

- 5. During training, we only require the blood pressure measurement at the outlet side of the domain; no extra measurement is needed.
